images.alt: Lesbeeld: de vijand eten geven — Romeinen 12:20; tekstillustratie.
images.prompt: Use case: historical-scene. Photorealistic illustration of an explicit biblical comparison or event, first-century Roman Judea and Galilee, landscape 3:2, natural materials and daylight, anatomically coherent people with exactly two arms and animals with correct limbs; fully covering modest opaque robes. No modern objects, readable writing, portrait of God the Father, blood, injury or watermark. Illustrate the ethical instruction of Romans 12:20, not a documented event. Two adult men who had been opponents sit at a simple outdoor table. One man gently places a bowl of food and cup of water before a hungry weary man; the hungry man is surprised, their expressions restrained and reconciliatory. No glowing coals on any head: that is a metaphor. Exactly two arms per person, clear simple hands and modest first-century clothes.

images.alt: Lesbeeld: een gave voor Jeruzalem — Romeinen 15:26; tekstillustratie.
images.prompt: Use case: historical-scene. Photorealistic illustration of an explicit biblical comparison or event, first-century Roman Judea and Galilee, landscape 3:2, natural materials and daylight, anatomically coherent people with exactly two arms and animals with correct limbs; fully covering modest opaque robes. No modern objects, readable writing, portrait of God the Father, blood, injury or watermark. Illustrate Romans 15:25–27, the voluntary financial collection by believers in Macedonia and Achaia for poor believers in Jerusalem. Small first-century household group places coins into a simple cloth purse on a table; an older woman and a younger adult man contribute while a responsible adult watches. This is preparation of material support, no temple offering altar and no modern charity logos. Use a Roman provincial domestic courtyard.

images.alt: Tertius schrijft de brief — Romeinen 16:22; tekstillustratie.
images.prompt: Use case: historical-scene. Photorealistic illustration of an explicit biblical comparison or event, first-century Roman Judea and Galilee, landscape 3:2, natural materials and daylight, anatomically coherent people with exactly two arms and animals with correct limbs; fully covering modest opaque robes. No modern objects, readable writing, portrait of God the Father, blood, injury or watermark. Romans 16:22 explicitly names Tertius as the person who wrote the letter. A first-century adult male scribe Tertius sits at a simple wooden table writing with a reed pen on an unrolled papyrus sheet; another adult man Paul speaks thoughtfully beside him. Side view where the papyrus writing cannot be read. Distinct two people, historically plausible ancient ink pot and papyrus, no codex or modern pen. The scene visualizes the named writing role; no claim to exact portraits.
